articles.title: ‘So big and so close’: going on a bear hunt in northern Spain
articles.summary: Conservationists have helped Cantabrian brown bears claw their way back from the edge of extinction in the beautiful mountains of Asturias – and carefully controlled nature tourism allows visitors to see them.
body: Once upon a time, in the woods outside Pola de Somiedo, lived a family of Cantabrian brown bears. The villagers reported sightings of a mother bear who had lost a leg to a hunter’s trap, her two cubs and two adult males, either of which might have been the father. In those days, at the end of the 1980s, they seemed to be the last of their kind in this part of Asturias. Meanwhile, the wider population dropped to about 60 bears across the surrounding Cantabrian mountain range that gave the species its name.

They have since clawed their way back from the edge of extinction here in northern Spain, and nature guide Luis Frechilla believes their numbers may now be upwards of 500 again. “They’re still classed as endangered,” he tells me, until the official count hits 1,000. But relative abundance makes them much easier to see today in Somiedo natural park – one of Spain’s first such protected areas, established in 1988.

articles.title: The pest I’ll never forget: the cockroaches were everywhere – even on our wine glasses
articles.summary: In a cheap London flat with no heating, dozens of the insects swarmed, leading to a Valentine’s Day that still makes me break out in a cold sweat. I don’t know if cockroaches really could, as we’re often told, survive a nuclear apocalypse, but I can tell you this with certainty: they can definitely…
body: It was January 2003 when I moved with my girlfriend Helen into our first London flat. It’s fair to say there were red flags we probably should have spotted. It was suspiciously affordable – £140 a week for a place less than a minute’s walk from Finsbury Park tube station? Sure, the place looked pretty skanky, but it was still spacious for a studio flat. We put the price down to the fact there was absolutely no way of heating the property and signed up.
That winter was bleak – we were freezing cold and, worse, waking up each morning with lines of red bites down our arms and legs. It took us a while to work out the culprits: bedbugs.

Bug spray was deployed, but it just made them angrier – the bites actually got worse. We replaced the mattress and that problem disappeared. (Despite not having encountered bedbugs anywhere since, Helen still checks down the the headboards in every hotel she stays at and won’t let her kids leave their bags on the floor.) The true horror, though, was yet to come.

articles.title: José Pizarro’s recipe for grilled sardines with blackberry escabeche
articles.summary: A winning combination of oily fish, sweet berries and a sharp dressing. One of my favourite summer memories is making collares de moras as a child in Extremadura, which involved threading wild blackberries on to a piece of straw to make little necklaces.
body: Heat a tablespoon of the oil, then gently fry the shallots and bell pepper for six or seven minutes, until lovely and tender. Add the thyme and spices, fry for a minute more, then add the vinegar, wine and 100ml water, bring to a simmer and cook until the liquid has reduced by about half. Stir in the blackberries, then take off the heat and leave to cool slightly.

Meanwhile, put the rest of the oil in a large nonstick frying pan on a high heat. Season the butterflied sardines inside and out, then fry them skin-side down for three or four minutes, until golden and crisp. Flip over and fry for just a minute longer on the flesh side.

Arrange the cooked sardines skin-side up and side by side in a suitable deep-sided dish, pour the warm escabeche all over the top, then leave to marinate and cool down for at least an hour. Serve at once, or cover and chill in the fridge until you’re ready to eat.
points: A winning combination of oily fish, sweet berries and a sharp dressing.

articles.title: Fashion’s New Instagram Playbook, According to Eva Chen
articles.summary: Instagram’s fashion whisperer shares the new rules of engagement, as shifting consumer expectations reshape how brands must show up both on and offline.
body: A decade into Instagram’s reign over fashion, keeping pace with the changing platform and the ways people use it has become something of a holy grail for fashion marketers. But lately, the conversation has become about much more than reach or engagement.

Virality has lost some of its luster; some people are retreating to smaller, niche platforms where there’s still room to be “messy” online; influencers are burning out, while brands are investing in real-world communities as consumers tire of life mediated through a screen. And yet, for all the talk of a social media backlash, we’re hardly logging off: in the UK, time spent on Instagram has risen by 60% in the last two years according to Ofcom, and Gen Z adults in the US spend an average of an hour a day on the platform, per Emarketer’s count.
points: Instagram’s fashion whisperer shares the new rules of engagement, as shifting consumer expectations reshape how brands must show up both on and offline.

articles.title: A health MOT is just one step towards prevention | Letters
articles.summary: Tackling social and economic conditions must come first, writes Dr Louise Lawson. Plus letters from James Hibberd, Bob Forster and Dr Giles Youngs. Devi Sridhar is right to welcome free cholesterol testing on the NHS in England and blood pressure checks in pharmacies.
body: Sridhar’s proposed five-point health MOT is undoubtedly valuable, but it is better understood as identifying risk rather than preventing disease. Prevention is what comes next: enabling people to make changes that improve health and reduce that risk. Public health has long distinguished between upstream factors, such as poverty, housing, employment, access to affordable healthy food and safe green spaces, and downstream interventions focused on individuals. Screening and health checks sit much closer to the downstream end of that spectrum.

Interventions aimed at changing behaviour emphasise individual responsibility and often assume that everyone has similar economic, social and psychological resources to adopt healthier lifestyles. Yet those living on low incomes, in insecure work or facing linguistic and cultural barriers often have far less capacity to act on health advice. Such approaches can also reinforce stigma by implying that poor health results primarily from individual choices rather than the circumstances in which people live, while diverting attention from the drivers of health inequalities.
points: Tackling social and economic conditions must come first, writes Dr Louise Lawson.

articles.title: A New Luxury Marketplace Is Making Adaptive Fashion More Discoverable
articles.summary: Weldun founder and CEO Carly Berlin’s new marketplace is built on the premise that functional clothing exists in luxury already — and can be big business.
body: Before her preventative double mastectomy, artist and designer Carly Berlin’s favorite brand to shop was Kallmeyer. Post-double mastectomy, Kallmeyer remained a favorite, thanks to the adaptability of many of the brand’s garments.

“Just because something is functional doesn’t mean that it can’t be beautiful. You see that all the time in interior design, but it’s really not a part of the conversation in fashion,” Berlin says. Recovering from her surgery, she wondered why the tie between functionality and beauty remained so underexamined in fashion. She connected with other women going through surgeries, treatments, and moments of physical change — and nobody knew where to look for fashion in these moments.

In the wake of her mastectomy, Berlin lived in Skims and Negative Underwear — and then gifted those same pieces to friends going through their own transitionary moments. After sending so many of her contacts the pieces she had discovered during hours of searching, Berlin decided to create the discovery layer for pieces that are tasteful, beautiful, and, most importantly, wearable.
points: Weldun founder and CEO Carly Berlin’s new marketplace is built on the premise that functional clothing exists in luxury already — and can be big business.

articles.title: Fine Jewelry’s Newest Discovery Channel? TikTok
articles.summary: Sophie Whitelaw found online fame designing jewelry online. It’s helped grow her brand and is propelling other businesses in the same way.
body: British jeweler Sophie Whitelaw first went viral on TikTok in 2025 while documenting the design of her own engagement ring — an emerald-cut natural diamond band surrounded by lab-grown stones — for tens of thousands of viewers. As a gemologist and founder of her eponymous, independent fine jewelry brand, she offered a rare insider’s view of a process most customers don’t see.

The business was three years old by then, its growth built on an early bet on TikTok as a discovery channel. Whitelaw launched her business in 2022, getting her start by designing bespoke rings for people she knew.

“It got to the point where I’d run out of friends and family to make pieces for, so I went to TikTok because I didn’t have a marketing budget,” she told Vogue Business. Its algorithm offered bigger reach, especially geographically, and early anonymity.
points: Sophie Whitelaw found online fame designing jewelry online.
It’s helped grow her brand and is propelling other businesses in the same way.

articles.title: The Best Kitchen Composter Actually Makes Compost With No Stench or Mess
articles.summary: Electric composting machines and food recyclers promise to turn food scraps into grounds with zero stench and minimal cleanup. Here are the ones we recommend.
body: I consider myself a fairly eco-conscious person. I reduce, reuse, recycle; I take public transit; I avoid using AI for meme-making and learning celebrity heights. But composting never really took. I'd try to gather food scraps in a plastic countertop compost bin in my kitchen, but emptying and cleaning the receptacle every couple days was messy and smelly and I'd give up after a couple weeks. In 2025, however, New York City made composting the law of the land and I knew I needed to figure out a more sustainable solution.

Electric kitchen composters and food recyclers promise to turn your food scraps into dried grounds or usable compost in a matter of hours, eliminating the need to transport a dripping bag of rotting food goo through your apartment and around the block to where your building keeps the communal bin (just me?). Like magic, these machines can reduce the volume of your food waste by up to 90%, so you can go weeks or months without emptying them. The downside? Many of them are very expensive.
points: Electric composting machines and food recyclers promise to turn food scraps into grounds with zero stench and minimal cleanup.
